sections.3:
Return the lexicographically smallest [i,j], i<j, whose values sum to target; return [] when no pair exists.

**API:** solve(values,target); C++ two_sum. Sorted nondecreasing signed values ±10^9, n≤10000; target ±2*10^9. Indices are zero-based and refer to the unchanged input.

[Shared contracts](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-conventions.md) specify numeric/byte domains, invalid-input behavior, resource bounds and exact CLI grammar.
sections.8:
Validate type, size, numeric bounds, target and nondecreasing order. Initialize left=0,right=n-1. Increase left for a sum below target and decrease right above target. On equality, move right leftward across equal right values while keeping right>left, then return the pair. If pointers meet/cross, return [].

**Correctness:** Every discarded left value has no valid partner in the remaining interval because its largest possible sum is too small. Every discarded right value has no partner at or beyond the current left because its smallest possible sum is too large. Thus the first surviving equality has the smallest possible left index. Equal right values yield the same sum; shrinking across their suffix chooses the earliest valid right index. This proves the specified lexicographic pair while preserving all feasible candidates until found.
sections.9:
```text
validate sorted array and target
left=0; right=n-1
while left<right:
    s=values[left]+values[right]
    if s<target: left+=1
    else if s>target: right-=1
    else:
        while right>left+1 and values[right-1]=values[right]: right-=1
        return [left,right]
return []
```
sections.10: For [1,1,2,2] and target 3, the first equality is at [0,3]. The equal right-hand 2 at index 2 is earlier, so return [0,2]. For [2,2,2] and target 4, return [0,1]. An empty array has right=-1 and never enters the loop.
sections.11: The scan is O(n) worst case because left only increases and right only decreases, including duplicate shrinking. Numeric/sorted validation scans input even if the first pair matches, so the public API has O(n) valid-array work overall (O(1) for empty/minimal sizes), rather than claiming best O(1) while ignoring validation.
sections.12: O(1) auxiliary scan/validation state and at most two returned indices; no sort, hash table or copied input array is used by the algorithm.
sections.16:
Empty/singleton arrays, duplicates, repeated zeros, negative operands, target at either bound and impossible pairs are defined. Unsorted input is rejected instead of silently sorted. Equal-valued positions must still have distinct indices; pointer crossing produces [].

[Python tests](tests/test_python.py) and [C++ tests](tests/test_cpp.py) exercise deterministic vectors, independent references and invalid contracts. Actual seeds/counts/results are recorded in [checkpoints](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-checkpoints.md).
sections.18: Sortedness is a real precondition and its validation cost is included. The API returns one earliest pair, not every pair or a count of duplicate pair combinations.
sections.24: [UCSD ICPC two-pointer/sliding-window lesson](https://ucsdicpc.github.io/slides/two_pointers_lesson.pdf). The exact index tie rule and validation policy are derived here. The bounded API and output/tie rules are repository contracts.

sections.3:
Return maximum values for windows [i,i+k) in input order, supporting arbitrary signed values and duplicates.

**API:** solve(values,k); C++ sliding_max. Values ±10^9, n≤10000. For nonempty input require 1≤k≤n; empty input requires k=0 and returns [].

[Shared contracts](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-conventions.md) specify numeric/byte domains, invalid-input behavior, resource bounds and exact CLI grammar.
sections.8:
Validate input and k before indexing. On each index, expire deque-front indices outside the window. Pop back candidates with value≤the new value, retaining the newest representative on equality. Append the new index. Once at least k values have arrived, append the front candidate value to the output.

**Correctness:** Deque indices increase, all candidates lie in the active window, and their values strictly decrease. Removing expired indices cannot affect a valid current window. Removing a dominated older candidate is safe for every future window containing it, because the newer candidate is at least as large and survives at least as long. Therefore the front is the active maximum. Every complete window is reported once after its right endpoint arrives.
sections.9:
```text
validate array/k; handle empty input
queue=[]; result=[]
for index in increasing order:
    remove front indices outside [index-k+1,index]
    while queue nonempty and values[back]<=values[index]: pop back
    push index
    if index+1>=k: append values[front]
return result
```
sections.10: For [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k=3, the first deque front is value 3. Sliding drops expired candidates and the arriving 5 dominates previous smaller values. Outputs are [3,3,5,5,6,7]. Equal maxima keep the later index, but only maximum values are returned.
sections.11: O(n) validation plus amortized deque work: each index is appended once and removed at most once. A single arrival can pop many candidates, but the total over the scan is linear. No random-input or nonnegative-sum assumption is needed. k=1 and k=n follow the same bound.
sections.12: O(k) auxiliary candidate indices and O(n-k+1) returned values for nonempty input. Empty input returns [] with constant work. No copy of each window is built.
sections.16:
Empty/k=0, one element, k=1, k=n, repeated equal values, increasing/decreasing arrays and all-negative arrays are tested. Empty with positive k, nonempty with zero k, k>n, negative k and invalid values are rejected. There are no partial windows in the output.

[Python tests](tests/test_python.py) and [C++ tests](tests/test_cpp.py) exercise deterministic vectors, independent references and invalid contracts. Actual seeds/counts/results are recorded in [checkpoints](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-checkpoints.md).
sections.18: This API returns values only, not argmax identities or partially filled windows. Deque memory can reach k on a decreasing array. It is a static eager scan, not a streaming object with a mutation interface.
sections.24: [UCSD two-pointer/sliding-window lesson](https://ucsdicpc.github.io/slides/two_pointers_lesson.pdf) and [Python deque documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.deque). The monotonic-candidate proof is derived explicitly here. The bounded API and output/tie rules are repository contracts.

sections.3:
Return the earliest longest half-open byte interval [start,end] with all distinct symbols, or [0,0] for empty input.

**API:** solve(text); C++ longest_distinct. Python bytes/C++ std::string, length≤10000, all 256 bytes supported. Unicode callers encode UTF-8 explicitly; indexes count bytes.

[Shared contracts](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-conventions.md) specify numeric/byte domains, invalid-input behavior, resource bounds and exact CLI grammar.
sections.8:
Validate bytes and length; initialize a 256-entry last-position table to -1. For each right index, set left=max(left,last[byte]+1), update last[byte], and compare the current interval length with the best. Replace best only for a strictly longer interval so the earliest equal-length answer remains.

**Correctness:** Before extension the active interval has unique bytes. The new byte can duplicate only its last occurrence; advancing beyond it removes that conflict, while max prevents reintroducing older conflicts by moving left backward. Thus each maintained interval is the longest unique suffix ending at the current right. Considering all right endpoints finds the global optimum. Right endpoints and left boundaries are nondecreasing, so keeping the first equal optimum implements earliest-start ties.
sections.9:
```text
last[0..255]=-1; left=0; best=[0,0]
for right,byte in text:
    left=max(left,last[byte]+1)
    last[byte]=right
    if right+1-left>best.length: best=[left,right+1]
return best
```
sections.10: For abba, after ab the best is [0,2]. The second b moves left to 2. The final a was previously at index 0, outside the active window; max keeps left=2 rather than incorrectly moving it backward to 1. ba ties the length two, so earliest ab remains [0,2].
sections.11: O(n+256) time including table initialization; for the fixed alphabet this is O(n+1). Each right index is processed once and left never retreats. No per-substring scan is used in production.
sections.12: O(256) auxiliary last-position entries and a two-index result, constant for the supported alphabet. No substring copies or returned text allocation are performed by the algorithm.
sections.16:
Empty, repeated bytes, alternating sequences, a repeated symbol already outside the window, earliest ties, NUL/255, all-byte alphabets and UTF-8-encoded samples are tested. Python str/bytearray and overlong input are rejected. UTF-8 intervals may split code points; no normalization or grapheme guarantee is implied.

[Python tests](tests/test_python.py) and [C++ tests](tests/test_cpp.py) exercise deterministic vectors, independent references and invalid contracts. Actual seeds/counts/results are recorded in [checkpoints](../../../docs/two-pointers-sliding-window-checkpoints.md).
sections.18: The alphabet is bytes, not Unicode code points or graphemes. The API returns one optimal interval, not all optimal spans or a copied substring.
sections.24: [UCSD sliding-window lesson](https://ucsdicpc.github.io/slides/two_pointers_lesson.pdf) and the repository’s [String byte contracts](../../../docs/string-conventions.md). The last-position invariant and earliest tie rule are derived here. The bounded API and output/tie rules are repository contracts.

sections.3: Each activity is an integer half-open interval [start,finish), with start<finish and both times in [-10^9,10^9]. At most 10000 activities are accepted. Touching endpoints are compatible. Return original zero-based indices in selection order. Sort ties by (finish,start,index). Duplicate intervals remain distinct input positions, but their positive durations prevent selecting overlapping copies together. Empty input returns []. Zero-duration and reversed intervals are rejected.
sections.8:
Validate the intervals, sort their indices by (finish,start,index), and begin with no previous finish. Accept an index when its start is at least the last chosen finish, then advance that finish. Rejecting an overlapping activity never invalidates an earlier choice.

Greedy-choice exchange: let g be the earliest-finishing compatible activity and let o be the first activity in an optimal remaining schedule. Since finish(g)≤finish(o), replacing o by g preserves every later activity and does not reduce count. The remainder after g has the same problem form, so optimal substructure and induction prove maximum cardinality. Equal-finish choices leave identical future availability; start/index ties make the output deterministic without altering the optimum. The scan invariant is that selected activities are compatible and the chosen prefix can extend to an optimum for the unprocessed choices.
sections.9:
```text
order ← original indices sorted by (finish,start,index)
selected ← []; last_finish ← absent
for i in order:
    if last_finish absent OR start[i] ≥ last_finish:
        append i to selected
        last_finish ← finish[i]
return selected
```
sections.10:
Input indices and intervals: 0:[1,3), 1:[2,5), 2:[3,4), 3:[4,7), 4:[5,6).

| Sorted index | Interval | Last finish before | Decision |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | [1,3) | absent | choose; finish=3 |
| 2 | [3,4) | 3 | choose; finish=4 |
| 1 | [2,5) | 4 | skip overlap |
| 4 | [5,6) | 4 | choose; finish=6 |
| 3 | [4,7) | 6 | skip overlap |

Return [0,2,4], count 3. A different maximum schedule can exist, but the specified key determines this one.
sections.11: For n activities, validation and selection each take O(n), while sorting takes O(n log(n+1)) worst time. Total worst time is O(n log(n+1)); sorting dominates. Python adaptive sorting can make already ordered inputs O(n); C++ std::sort retains its O(n log(n+1)) comparison bound without a stronger best-case promise. Average time needs an input distribution; none is assumed. If a separately validated input is already sorted, the selection step itself is linear.
sections.12: O(n) auxiliary index storage plus up to O(n) output indices. Python sorting may use O(n) temporary storage; C++ sorting typically needs O(log n) stack within the O(n) total bound. Original intervals are not copied or mutated. A caller that already maintains finishing order could stream the selection with O(1) scan state plus output.
sections.16: Empty input returns []; one valid activity is selected. Fully overlapping input yields one activity. Touching intervals can all be selected. Negative time coordinates are supported; no special zero origin is assumed. Duplicate intervals use the earliest original index after equal finish/start. Validation rejects nonintegers, start≥finish, out-of-range coordinates and n=10001. Independent tests enumerate every positional subset, verify compatibility and maximize its count, then apply the stated deterministic order among optima.
sections.18: Only one resource and equal activity rewards are modeled. Earliest finish does not generally maximize weighted reward: [0,1) and [1,2), each reward 1, beat a single count-wise choice [0,2) but lose to it if its reward is 100. The 10000-item cap is an educational resource contract. Time values are compared rather than subtracted, so no overflow-sensitive duration calculation is needed.
sections.24: [MIT 6.046: Overview and Interval Scheduling](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-046j-design-and-analysis-of-algorithms-spring-2015/resources/lecture-1-course-overview-interval-scheduling/) provides original course material on interval scheduling and greedy analysis. This implementation and its numeric/tie contracts are project-specific; no lecture code is copied.

sections.3: The alphabet contains unique integer bytes 0..255 and frequencies in 1..10^9. Python accepts a mapping; C++ accepts unique symbol/frequency pairs and rejects duplicates. Empty alphabet produces no codes and accepts only an empty message/stream. A singleton uses code "0", not an empty codeword. Heap ties are (frequency,minimum byte in subtree,creation index), with leaves created in ascending byte order; the first popped child receives 0, the second 1. APIs expose codewords, weighted bit cost, encoding and decoding. Messages are at most 10000 bytes and bit strings at most 1000000 bits; decoded output also has the 10000-byte cap.
sections.8:
Validate symbols/frequencies, create one leaf per symbol and push its heap key. Repeatedly pop the two minimum keys, append a parent node with summed weight and minimum subtree byte, and push the parent key. Continue until one root remains. Traverse left/right as 0/1 to assign leaf codes; use 0 for a singleton. Encoding concatenates known-symbol codewords after size checks. Decoding walks the tree until a leaf emits one byte and restarts at the root; nonbinary bits, invalid singleton bits, incomplete final paths and oversized outputs are rejected.

Greedy-choice proof: an optimal full binary tree has a deepest sibling-leaf pair. Exchanging the two smallest-weight symbols into those deepest positions cannot increase weighted path length. Collapse them to a leaf with their sum; expanding any collapsed solution increases cost by exactly that sum. Thus optimal substructure holds and induction proves the repeated two-minimum construction optimal. This argument applies to k≥2. The k=1 cost is frequency under the explicitly required nonempty-codeword convention. Distinct leaves cannot be ancestors of one another, proving prefix freedom; walking complete leaf paths proves round-trip correctness.
sections.9:
```text
heap ← one (frequency,minimum_symbol,node_index) entry per leaf
while heap contains at least two entries:
    left ← pop_min(heap); right ← pop_min(heap)
    parent ← node(left,right) with summed frequency
    push(heap,parent_key)
traverse root, appending 0 on left and 1 on right
encode: concatenate code[byte] for each known message byte
decode: follow each bit; emit at a leaf and restart at root
reject if final decoder position is inside a codeword
```
sections.10:
Frequencies A(65)=5, B(66)=2, C(67)=1:

| Step | Heap weights before | Merge | Heap after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | C:1, B:2, A:5 | C left + B right → CB:3 | CB:3, A:5 |
| 2 | CB:3, A:5 | CB left + A right → root:8 | root:8 |

The resulting codes are A=1, B=01, C=00. Weighted cost is 5·1+2·2+1·2=11. Message ABCA encodes as 1|01|00|1 = 101001. Following that stream reaches leaves A,B,C,A and ends at the root. With four equal symbols A..D the deterministic codes are 00,01,10,11.
sections.11: Let k be alphabet size, L the sum of codeword lengths, m message bytes and B encoded bits. Tree construction performs k-1 heap merges, giving O(k log(k+1)) worst time after leaf ordering. Materializing all code strings costs O(k+L), so total codebook construction is O(k log(k+1)+L); L can be O(k²) for skewed trees. Encoding in Python is O(m+B) expected dictionary work; C++ ordered-map lookup adds O(m log(k+1)). Decoding is O(B+output bytes). Empty operations take O(1). No input distribution for an average build time is assumed; the same worst bounds apply. Singleton code generation is constant-sized regardless of its frequency.
sections.12: The tree/heap occupy O(k) nodes/entries. Codes use O(k+L) storage; recursive traversal has depth at most k-1 (at most 255), and temporary prefixes remain within the O(k+L) bound. Encoding adds O(m+B), decoding O(output bytes), excluding input storage. Python codebook access returns an owned dictionary copy with immutable string values; C++ returns a const map reference. No bits are packed into machine-byte output.
sections.16: Empty alphabet/message is valid; nonempty data with no alphabet is rejected. A singleton encodes each occurrence as 0 and rejects 1. Equal frequencies, embedded byte zero, byte 255, repeated message bytes, skewed powers-of-two frequencies and the full 256-byte alphabet are tested. Frequencies must be strictly positive, finite native integers, not zero or negative. Unknown symbols, duplicates in C++/CLI, nonbinary strings and truncated codewords are errors. Tests exhaustively enumerate every pair choice in small merge trees, not just the greedy merge order, to obtain independent optimum weighted costs.
sections.18: These are ordinary deterministic Huffman tree codes, **not canonical Huffman codes** ordered by code lengths. The frequency table/tree must be shared by encoder and decoder; raw bit strings contain no header or integrity check. Input is bytes, not Unicode characters; callers choose any text-to-byte encoding separately. Node sums are ≤256·10^9; weighted cost is conservatively ≤256·10^9·255, below signed-64. Resource caps are validated. String-bit output is educational and may be larger in memory than the original bytes; no compression-ratio claim is made for this representation.
sections.24: David A. Huffman, [A Method for the Construction of Minimum-Redundancy Codes (1952)](https://www.cse.iitd.ac.in/~pkalra/siv864/huffman_1952.pdf), is the original construction paper. [ETH Zürich Greedy Algorithms](https://lec.inf.ethz.ch/DA/2017/slides/daLecture15.en.handout.pdf) gives course context. The code, byte-domain limits, tie rules and singleton convention here are independently specified; no source code is copied.

sections.3: Given n≤10000 positive integer weights in 1..10^6, nonnegative integer values in 0..10^6 and integer capacity C in 0..10^9, choose fractions f_i in [0,1] maximizing sum(v_i f_i), subject to sum(w_i f_i)≤C. Return (exact total value, one exact fraction per original item). Python uses Fraction; C++ uses reduced nonnegative numerator/denominator pairs in KnapsackResult. Zero/negative weights and negative values are rejected. Zero-value items remain unselected, even if capacity remains. Equal ratios prefer the earlier original position.
sections.8:
Validate equal lengths and all domains. Sort original indices using cross products, then original-index ties. Start all fractions at zero and capacity unchanged. Take min(weight,remaining) from each positive-value item and record its reduced fraction. Add the corresponding exact value; stop at zero remaining capacity or zero density.

Greedy-choice proof: if a feasible allocation uses some lower-density weight while a higher-density item is not full, transfer equal weight to the latter. Capacity is unchanged and value does not decrease; it increases for unequal densities. Repeating this exchange yields a density-ordered prefix with at most one partial item. Equal-density transfers favor earlier indices as specified. After filling a prefix, the remaining capacity and remaining items form the same optimization problem, proving optimal substructure. Zero-value items may be omitted without lowering value.
sections.9:
```text
order ← indices sorted by descending exact value/weight, then index
fractions[0..n-1] ← 0; total ← 0; remaining ← C
for i in order:
    if remaining=0 OR value[i]=0: break
    take ← min(weight[i],remaining)
    fractions[i] ← exact_fraction(take,weight[i])
    total ← total + value[i]*fractions[i]
    remaining ← remaining-take
return total,fractions
```
sections.10:
For weights [10,20,30], values [60,100,120], capacity 50:

| Item | Density | Remaining before | Fraction | Added value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 6 | 50 | 1 | 60 |
| 1 | 5 | 40 | 1 | 100 |
| 2 | 4 | 20 | 2/3 | 80 |

The final value is 240 and fractions [1,1,2/3]. The fraction is needed: selecting only whole items cannot produce this allocation. With weight 3, value 2 and capacity 1, the exact total is 2/3, not a rounded decimal.
sections.11: Validation and output initialization are O(n); sorting and selection give O(n log(n+1)) worst time with O(n) scan work. Python sorting can be linear on already ordered ratios; C++ std::sort provides an O(n log(n+1)) comparison bound. No average distribution is assumed. GCD reduction and ratio comparisons operate on the documented bounded integers; if the caps are removed, bit-complexity costs must also be included.
sections.12: O(n) auxiliary sorted indices and O(n) fraction output; no algorithm recursion. Python sorting may allocate O(n) temporary space. Exact rational values use bounded words in C++ under this contract. The input is not mutated; streaming without sorting would require density-ordered input.
sections.16: Empty input returns value 0 and []. Zero capacity returns all-zero fractions. If capacity exceeds all positive-value weight, take all positive-value items and leave zero-value ones at zero. Equal density is deterministic by original index. Invalid weights are rejected even when capacity is zero. Tests independently enumerate all small LP vertices: each has zero/one fractions except at most one partial item, then maximize exact objective and the stated allocation tie policy.
sections.18: Fractional selection is essential; using this strategy for indivisible 0/1 items is incorrect. The API excludes zero-weight “free value” items, negative values, real-valued inputs and nonlinear constraints. Density cross products are ≤10^12. Full-item value is ≤10^10; a total rational numerator is at most 10^10·10^6+10^12, below signed-64, with denominator≤10^6. No floating point is used internally. Converting results to float externally can round, so preserve numerator/denominator pairs for exactness.
sections.24: [ETH Zürich: Greedy Algorithms lecture handout](https://lec.inf.ethz.ch/DA/2017/slides/daLecture15.en.handout.pdf) covers fractional knapsack, Activity Selection and Huffman Coding. This exact-rational API, input caps and deterministic allocation are independently specified here; no lecture implementation is copied.

sections.3: All jobs are independent, available from time zero and take exactly one unit. Slot s is [s-1,s), so a job in slot s meets deadline d when s≤d. Deadlines are integers 0..10^9; deadline zero is valid but unschedulable, negative deadlines are invalid. Profits are integers in [-10^9,10^9]; nonpositive-profit jobs are omitted. Equal positive profits prefer lower original index. Accept n≤10000 with equal deadline/profit lengths. Return (total profit,slots), where each slot is an original job index or None/null. The fixed returned horizon is H=min(n,max(deadlines,default=0)); even unused trailing slots remain represented.
sections.8:
Validate domains and allocate slots/parent/rank/available arrays for 0..H. Each initial component has available[s]=s. A component represents an occupied consecutive block plus its left free boundary; store that boundary independently of the representative chosen by union rank. Query available[find(min(deadline,H))]. If nonzero, write the job index to that slot and union its component with find(slot-1), keeping the smaller available boundary. Path compression and rank keep queries efficient without changing the boundary meaning.

Correctness of feasibility: latest placement preserves earlier capacity. If no slot is free before d, expanding the saturated prefix to cover the capped deadlines of its occupants yields a saturated prefix ending T whose T occupants must all finish by T. Adding the candidate would require T+1 completions by T, impossible. Thus the slot structure accepts exactly feasible additions.

Greedy-choice/exchange: feasible unit-job subsets obey the nested capacity constraints count(deadline≤t)≤t for every t. This family is hereditary. For feasible A,B with |A|<|B|, if no b in B\A can augment A, each such b lies in an A-tight prefix. Their largest tight prefix contains all B\A; feasibility of B then forces |B\A|≤|A\B|, a contradiction. This is the exchange property of a matroid. Its weighted greedy exchange lets the next highest-profit feasible job replace a no-more-profitable unchosen job in an optimum; previously chosen jobs stay fixed. Induction proves maximum profit. Omitting nonpositive profits cannot decrease it. Clamping deadlines to n is safe because at most n jobs can be scheduled.
sections.9:
```text
H ← min(n, maximum deadline or 0)
initialize disjoint sets 0..H, each with its own free boundary
slots[1..H] ← empty; total ← 0
for i in positive-profit, positive-deadline jobs sorted by (-profit,index):
    s ← available[find(min(deadline[i],H))]
    if s>0:
        slots[s] ← i; total ← total+profit[i]
        union components of s and s-1 using rank/path compression
        new component available ← minimum of their available boundaries
return total,slots
```
sections.10:
Jobs 0:(d=2,p=100), 1:(1,19), 2:(2,27), 3:(1,25), 4:(3,15), H=3:

| Profit-order job | Latest free ≤ deadline | Slots after | Profit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 2 | [empty,0,empty] | 100 |
| 2 | 1 | [2,0,empty] | 127 |
| 3 | none | [2,0,empty] | 127 |
| 1 | none | [2,0,empty] | 127 |
| 4 | 3 | [2,0,4] | 142 |

All selected completion slots meet their deadlines and each original position appears once. Return profit 142 and slots [2,0,4].
sections.11: Let n be input jobs, q eligible positive jobs and H≤n the horizon. Validation and initialization cost O(n+H); sorting costs O(q log(q+1)). Union by rank with path compression gives O(q·α(H+1)) amortized slot operations, where α is the inverse Ackermann function. Total worst upper bound is O(n log(n+1)), independent of the numerical magnitude of deadlines. When q=0, the work is O(n+H); sorting can adapt to order in Python. No probability distribution is assumed for an average-case number. A backwards linear slot scan would instead take O(nH) worst time.
sections.12: O(n+H) auxiliary indices/disjoint-set arrays plus O(H) returned optional indices; H≤n. No recursion is used in find, so long chains do not consume the Python call stack. Keeping available separately from the representative allows rank balancing while preserving the latest-free-slot meaning. Input profits/deadlines are not mutated.
sections.16: Empty input gives (0,[]). All zero deadlines produce an empty horizon. Nonpositive jobs are omitted; their deadlines can still contribute to the documented fixed horizon. Duplicate deadlines compete for slots and equal profits prefer lower original index. With deadlines [2,2], profits [5,5], slots are [1,0] because job 0 takes the latest slot first. Huge sparse deadlines are clamped before allocation. Independent tests enumerate every small job subset and use sorted-deadline feasibility, then compare optimal profit and verify each returned witness.
sections.18: The exchange proof relies on unit duration, one machine, no release times and independent jobs. It does not solve arbitrary-duration weighted interval scheduling. Nonpositive profits are intentionally not used to fill idle slots. Total positive profit is at most 10000·10^9=10^13, safely within signed-64; deadlines are clamped before conversion to slot sizes. The 10000-job cap is explicit. Different equal-profit rules could return different optimal schedules.
sections.24: [CLRS-Lean: A Task-Scheduling Problem as a Matroid](https://tanktechnology.github.io/CLRS-Lean/CLRSLean/Chapter_16/Section_16_5_Task_Scheduling/) is original formalization work on unit-task deadlines and the scheduling matroid. This profit-maximizing API and ranked latest-slot implementation are independently specified and proved above; no external implementation is copied.

sections.3: For an integer index n, return F(n), where F(0)=0, F(1)=1, and F(n)=F(n-1)+F(n-2) for n≥2. The shared API supports 0≤n≤92. Negative/noninteger indices are invalid; n>92 raises overflow even in Python so the languages agree.
sections.8:
Return zero for n=0. Start previous=F(0), current=F(1). For i=2..n, compute next=previous+current, then advance both states. Before iteration i, the states are F(i-2),F(i-1); the recurrence makes the new pair F(i-1),F(i). Induction proves current=F(n) at termination. No unnecessary F(93) is computed when n=92.

Memoization caches recursive calls using O(n) storage and stack. Full tabulation stores F(0..n). The implemented rolling tabulation keeps only the live dependency window.
sections.9:
```text
if n = 0: return 0
previous ← 0; current ← 1
for i ← 2 through n:
    next ← previous + current
    previous ← current
    current ← next
return current
```
sections.10:
For n=6, the conceptual DP table is:

| i | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F(i) | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 5 | 8 |

At i=4, (previous,current)=(1,2), so next=3. The final pair is (5,8); return 8. n=0 takes its direct base-case return.
sections.11: With n the index, the generalized operation count is Θ(n) for n≥2 and Θ(1) for n=0,1; input order does not affect it. The implementation caps n at 92, making each addition a bounded-word operation. Removing the numeric cap would require bit-complexity accounting, not merely a claim of O(n) machine time.
sections.12: O(1) auxiliary integer words, O(1) output words and no recursion stack. CLI input token storage is separate from algorithm workspace. Full tabulation/memoization use O(n) words; rolling states are the implemented space optimization.
sections.16: F(0)=0 and F(1)=1. F(92)=7540113804746346429 fits signed 64-bit; F(93)=12200160415121876738 does not. Both APIs reject negative indices and reject 93 before arithmetic. Tests cover every allowed index using an independent binomial-sum identity for tilings.
sections.18: The shared API intentionally does not provide arbitrary-precision Fibonacci. Fixed-width C++ overflow must never be treated as wraparound. Two rolling states do not retain all preceding sequence values.

sections.3: Return maximum value only, with empty selection allowed. weights and values have equal lengths n≤1000; capacity C is in 0..10000 and n(C+1)≤2000000. Weights are integers in 0..10^9; values are in [-10^9,10^9]. Negative values are valid and may be omitted. Duplicate weights represent distinct items. Zero weights are valid.
sections.8:
Base D(0,c)=0. For item (w,v), D(i,c)=max(D(i-1,c),D(i-1,c-w)+v) when w≤c; otherwise copy the omission state. Update c from C down to w. For w>0, smaller cells still belong to the previous layer. For w=0, each cell is read and written once, so a positive zero-weight value is added once, including at capacity zero. An optimal subset either contains the current item or does not; the two exhaustive cases and induction prove optimality.

Memoization uses states (i,c) and a recursion stack. Tabulation visits items in increasing order. Rolling a single capacity row saves the item dimension; ascending capacities would instead allow repeated use.
sections.9:
```text
best[0..C] ← 0
for each (weight,value):
    for c ← C down through weight:
        best[c] ← max(best[c], best[c-weight]+value)
return best[C]
```
sections.10:
Items (2,3),(3,4),(4,5), capacity 5:

| Processed items / capacity | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| (2,3) | 0 | 0 | 3 | 3 | 3 | 3 |
| plus (3,4) | 0 | 0 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 7 |
| plus (4,5) | 0 | 0 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 7 |

The optimum 7 includes the first two items. The API returns 7, not their indices.
sections.11: Validation costs O(n); table initialization costs Θ(C+1). The recurrence work is at most O(n(C+1)), with no input-order benefit in the worst case. Items heavier than C perform no updates, so the best case is O(n+C+1). This is pseudo-polynomial in numeric capacity, not polynomial in its bit length.
sections.12: O(C+1) auxiliary words and O(1) scalar output; no recursive frames. The input occupies O(n). A full predecessor/item table would cost O(n(C+1)) and is unnecessary for a value-only answer. Reconstructing a selection needs additional bookkeeping or recomputation.
sections.16: Empty input returns 0 for any allowed capacity. Capacity zero still admits positive zero-weight items. Negative-valued items are skipped naturally. A single item of weight 1 and value 5 at capacity 2 returns 5, guarding against the unbounded-update defect. Exhaustive positional-subset oracles check randomized small instances.
sections.18: Capacity and work limits are part of the API and are checked before allocation. Values sum to at most 1000·10^9=10^12, so signed-64 additions are safe. This API does not return chosen items or solve fractional/unbounded/multidimensional variants.

sections.3: Return a length only, without reconstructing a sequence. Each string contains at most 1000 Unicode scalar values. Python strings containing lone surrogate code points are rejected; C++ accepts strict UTF-8 and decodes it before comparisons. No normalization, case folding, byte matching, or grapheme segmentation is performed. Empty strings are valid.
sections.8:
Base D(0,j)=D(i,0)=0. If a[i-1]=b[j-1], D(i,j)=D(i-1,j-1)+1. Otherwise D(i,j)=max(D(i-1,j),D(i,j-1)). For equal final symbols an optimum can match the final pair, with an optimal common prefix; for unequal symbols, a common subsequence cannot end at both unmatched positions. These exhaustive cases reduce prefix sizes, proving correctness by induction.

The implementation makes the shorter string the column dimension, then retains previous/current rows. Each current cell reads the previous diagonal, previous above, and current left. Memoization would cache the same (i,j) states with recursion; tabulation removes stack depth. Rolling rows save table storage but discard the path needed for reconstruction.
sections.9:
```text
choose shorter string as b
previous[0..len(b)] ← 0
for symbol x in a:
    current[0] ← 0
    for j ← 1..len(b):
        if x = b[j-1]: current[j] ← previous[j-1]+1
        else: current[j] ← max(previous[j],current[j-1])
    previous ← current
return previous[len(b)]
```
sections.10:
For a="abc", b="ac":

| a prefix / b prefix | empty | a | ac |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| empty | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| a | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| ab | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| abc | 0 | 1 | 2 |

At (3,2), final c matches c, so the diagonal value 1 becomes 2. The subsequence "ac" is noncontiguous in "abc", which rules out a substring interpretation.
sections.11: Let n,m be scalar-value counts and B UTF-8 byte count in C++. Validation/decoding is O(n+m) or O(B). DP performs Θ(nm) cell updates; including empty cases and row initialization, total time is O(nm+n+m+1). All arrangements of the same lengths visit the same table cells. Values are at most min(n,m)≤1000, so fixed-word arithmetic is safe.
sections.12: DP workspace is O(min(n,m)+1) words, with O(1) result and no recursion. Python reuses the original immutable strings. C++ additionally stores both decoded scalar arrays, so its total auxiliary storage is O(n+m+1), not just the rolling-row bound. Full tabulation or memoization uses O(nm) cells.
sections.16: Either empty string gives zero. Repeated symbols are matched in order and at most once per input position. "a😀ব" and "😀ব" have length 2. Precomposed "é" and decomposed "é" do not match because normalization is outside the contract. Tests intersect independently enumerated subsequence sets for exhaustive binary words and seeded Unicode cases; malformed UTF-8 and length 1001 are rejected.
sections.18: Quadratic work can be expensive for long text; the 1000-scalar cap bounds it to one million DP cells. No actual common sequence or edit script is returned. Equal-length optimal subsequences can differ, so reconstruction would need an explicit deterministic policy.

sections.3: Return a length only. Input contains n≤1000 native integers, each in [-10^9,10^9]. Empty input gives 0. Strictly increasing means each selected value is less than the next; equal values do not extend a sequence. Negative values are fully supported.
sections.8:
Initialize L(i)=1. Scan i from left to right and examine every j<i. If a[j]<a[i], try L(j)+1. Thus L(i)=1+max(L(j)) over feasible predecessors, or 1 if none exist. Every non-singleton increasing subsequence has a feasible final predecessor; taking its best prefix cannot worsen it. Every transition appends a larger value at a later position. Induction proves each L(i), then max_i L(i) is optimal.

Memoization would recursively evaluate predecessor states; iterative tabulation computes them in index order. The implemented table retains all endpoint values because any earlier endpoint can matter later. Two rolling scalars cannot represent them. A different tails-state formulation offers O(n log n) time but is not the implementation here.
sections.10:
For [3,1,2,2,4]:

| Position i | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Value | 3 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 4 |
| L(i) | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 |

The second 2 cannot extend the first 2. Position 4 can extend either length-2 endpoint, yielding length 3, for example [1,2,4].
sections.11: For n values, every pair j<i is compared, exactly n(n-1)/2 comparisons regardless of value ordering. Hence Θ(n²) time for n≥2 and Θ(n+1) for base-sized inputs, including validation/output handling. No O(n log n) claim is made for this code.
sections.12: O(n) auxiliary table words, O(1) result and no recursive stack. The input costs O(n). The O(n log n) tails alternative still uses O(n) worst-case workspace. Returning selected indices requires predecessor information, which this length-only API omits.
sections.16: Empty input gives 0; a singleton gives 1. All equal values give 1; strictly descending nonempty input gives 1. [-3,-2,-1] gives 3. Bounds ±10^9 are compared directly and never subtracted, avoiding arithmetic overflow. Independent exhaustive positional-subset tests cover duplicates and negatives.
sections.18: Quadratic runtime and the 1000-element cap limit practical size. The API does not reconstruct a witness, count optimal subsequences, or solve the non-decreasing variant. DP lengths are at most 1000 and fit signed-64 safely.

sections.3: Return a nonnegative distance only. Insertion, deletion and substitution each cost 1; leaving equal symbols matched costs 0. Inputs each contain at most 1000 Unicode scalar values. C++ decodes strict UTF-8; Python rejects surrogate code points. Normalization, case folding and grapheme segmentation are outside the contract.
sections.8:
Base D(i,0)=i and D(0,j)=j: deleting or inserting all symbols is necessary. Transition D(i,j)=min(D(i-1,j)+1, D(i,j-1)+1, D(i-1,j-1)+[a[i-1]≠b[j-1]]). Any optimal alignment has one of these final steps. Removing it leaves an optimal smaller-prefix problem; conversely each transition constructs a valid alignment. Induction on i+j proves the minimum.

Tabulation starts with row 0 as 0,1,..,m and sets the first cell of row i to i. Previous/current rows suffice because only above, left and diagonal are read. Unit symmetric costs allow swapping inputs to minimize row width. Memoization computes the same states recursively, but adds cache and stack overhead.
sections.9:
```text
previous ← [0,1,...,m]
for i ← 1..n:
    current[0] ← i
    for j ← 1..m:
        current[j] ← min(previous[j]+1, current[j-1]+1,
                         previous[j-1] + (a[i-1] ≠ b[j-1]))
    previous ← current
return previous[m]
```
sections.10:
For "cat" → "cut":

| source prefix / target prefix | empty | c | cu | cut |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| empty | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| c | 1 | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| ca | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| cat | 3 | 2 | 2 | 1 |

The optimum substitutes a→u once. For "kitten"→"sitting", substitute k→s, substitute e→i, then insert g, giving distance 3.
sections.11: With n,m scalar counts, total time is O(nm+n+m+1), including validation and initialization. C++ decoding costs O(B) for B UTF-8 bytes, at most four per scalar. The table cell count is independent of string contents, so fixed nonempty lengths give Θ(nm) DP work. Distances never exceed max(n,m)≤1000.
sections.12: O(min(n,m)+1) DP words and O(1) result, without recursive frames. C++ also stores O(n+m) decoded scalars, so total auxiliary storage there is O(n+m+1). Python uses original strings. A full matrix or memoization uses O(nm) cells; reconstruction requires more information than the returned distance.
sections.16: Empty-to-empty is zero. Empty-to-length-m is m; identical strings give zero. Repeated symbols are processed by position. "é" and "é" have distance 2 under the scalar contract, with no normalization. Transposing "ab" to "ba" costs 2. Independent tests enumerate all monotone paired-position alignments rather than reusing the DP recurrence.
sections.18: The implementation visits a quadratic state space and caps each string at 1000 scalars. It returns no edit script and does not implement weighted, affine-gap, transposition, or grapheme-aware distances. Invalid UTF-8 is rejected before table allocation.

sections.3: A dimension list [d0,d1,...,dn] represents n matrices Ai of shape di×d(i+1), using zero-based i. Shared adjacent dimensions guarantee compatibility by construction. Return minimum scalar cost only. [] denotes an empty chain and returns 0; length-one dimension lists are invalid; two dimensions describe one matrix and return 0. Allow at most 100 matrices, with each dimension an integer in 1..100000.
sections.8:
Base C(i,i)=0, since a single matrix needs no multiplication. For i<j, C(i,j)=min over i≤k<j of C(i,k)+C(k+1,j)+d_i·d_(k+1)·d_(j+1). Evaluate intervals by increasing length so every child interval is complete. Any parenthesization has exactly one final split; replacing either subtree with a lower-cost subtree preserves shape and lowers cost. Conversely each split combines valid subproducts. These exhaustive final splits and induction prove the optimum.

Memoization caches intervals recursively. Tabulation visits all intervals explicitly. Unlike a prefix-only recurrence, interval states need many shorter lengths, so two rolling rows do not retain all dependencies.
sections.9:
```text
C[i,i] ← 0
for length ← 2..n:
    for i ← 0..n-length:
        j ← i+length-1
        C[i,j] ← infinity
        for k ← i..j-1:
            candidate ← C[i,k]+C[k+1,j]+d[i]*d[k+1]*d[j+1]
            C[i,j] ← min(C[i,j],candidate)
return C[0,n-1], or 0 for no/single matrix
```
sections.11: For n matrices, O(n²) intervals each try O(n) splits, giving Θ(n³) work for n≥2. The exact split count is n(n-1)(n+1)/6. Input validation is O(n+1). Matrix values do not affect this dimension-only cost model, and no probabilistic average case is needed.
sections.12: O(n²) auxiliary integer cells, O(1) scalar output, and no recursive stack. Input dimensions use O(n). Triangular storage could reduce a constant factor; returning parenthesization would require a split table or recomputation.
sections.16: Empty [] and one matrix cost zero. A lone dimension does not describe a matrix and is rejected. Zero/negative, noninteger and oversized dimensions are rejected. Independently enumerated full binary parenthesizations verify small random chains, including equal dimensions. Separate boundary tests use 100 matrices of 100000×100000, with exact cost 99·10^15.
sections.18: Cubic runtime motivates the 100-matrix cap. Each scalar product cost is at most 10^15; a candidate tree has at most 99 products, so every intermediate addition is at most 99·10^15 and fits signed 64-bit. Python shares these bounds. Incompatible matrix-pair lists are not accepted: callers must supply the shared dimension-vector representation. No actual product or parenthesization is returned.

sections.3: Coins are positive integers in 1..10^9, with at most 1000 supplied entries. Duplicate denominations are collapsed and input order is irrelevant. Amount A is in 0..10000; supplied_count·(A+1)≤2000000. Any denomination may be used repeatedly. Minimum returns None/null when unreachable; counting returns zero. Amount zero has minimum zero and exactly one combination, the empty multiset.
sections.8:
M(0)=0; unreachable positive amounts start at A+1. For a>0, M(a)=min(1+M(a-c)) over c≤a, with unreachable states ignored by the sentinel. Removing the last coin yields a smaller amount; induction proves the minimum.

For counting, W(0,0)=1 and W(0,a>0)=0. W(k,a)=W(k-1,a)+W(k,a-c_k) when a≥c_k. The first term excludes the denomination; removing one copy from the second case is a bijection to the smaller amount. These cases are disjoint. Use denominations outside, amounts increasing inside. Memoization could cache these same states; tabulation avoids recursive depth. One amount row suffices for each API.
sections.10:
For coins 1,3,4 and A=6:

| Amount | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| minimum | 0 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 |
| ways after coin 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| ways after coin 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| ways after coin 4 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 4 |

Amount 6 combinations are six 1s, three 1s plus 3, two 3s, and two 1s plus 4. Reordering the same coins does not add combinations.
sections.11: Let n be supplied count and k distinct count. Sorting/deduplication costs O(n log(n+1)); DP worst time is O(kA+A+1) for each API. Minimum visits all coin checks for every positive amount. Counting skips denominations larger than A, so may take O(A+k) recurrence work in that case. Numeric A makes the bound pseudo-polynomial.
sections.12: O(A+k+1) auxiliary words including deduplicated denominations, with scalar output and no recursion. A two-dimensional count table uses O(kA) storage; the implemented increasing update saves the denomination dimension. Returning both answers in the CLI evaluates the two APIs separately.
sections.16: No denominations at amount zero gives [0,1]; at a positive amount it gives [null,0]. [2] cannot make 3. [1,2,2] counts like [1,2]. Zero/negative denominations are rejected, preventing nonterminating or undefined unlimited-copy interpretations. Tests enumerate multiplicities independently, rather than repeating either DP.
sections.18: Minimum values are at most A. Combination counts grow rapidly: both languages raise on any counting-table addition above 2^63-1, even if that intermediate amount is not the final request. Python deliberately shares this limit. No modular, arbitrary-precision, bounded-inventory, or ordered-permutation mode is implied.

sections.3: Accept n≤1000 integers in 0..10^9 and target T in 0..10000, with n(T+1)≤2000000. Negative values and targets are rejected. The empty subset is allowed, so target zero always succeeds after validation. Duplicates represent different selectable positions. Return bool, not selected indices or the number of solutions.
sections.8:
Base R(0,0)=true and R(0,t>0)=false. For value v, R(i,t)=R(i-1,t) OR R(i-1,t-v) when t≥v; otherwise retain omission. Update t downward so the remainder belongs to the previous item layer. Zero values read the same cell once and do not change existence. Any valid subset either contains the newest position or does not, and both transitions construct valid subsets, proving correctness by induction over items.

Memoization could cache (i,t) with recursive inclusion/exclusion. Tabulation retains only the previous item layer. A descending one-dimensional row is the implemented space optimization; ascending updates would permit repeatedly using a position.
sections.9:
```text
reachable[0] ← true; reachable[1..T] ← false
for value in values:
    for t ← T down through value:
        reachable[t] ← reachable[t] OR reachable[t-value]
return reachable[T]
```
sections.10:
For values [2,3,2] and T=4:

| Processed values / total | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| none | true | false | false | false | false |
| first 2 | true | false | true | false | false |
| plus 3 | true | false | true | true | false |
| second 2 | true | false | true | true | true |

The final 4 uses both distinct 2 positions. With just [2], total 4 remains false; descending traversal prevents accidental unlimited reuse.
sections.11: Validation takes O(n), initialization O(T+1), and updates at most O(n(T+1)). Worst total time is O(nT+n+T+1). Values larger than T perform no updates, giving O(n+T+1) in that case. This bound is pseudo-polynomial in numeric target. No input-order average is assumed.
sections.12: O(T+1) Boolean cells and O(1) output, no recursive stack. Python stores Boolean references; C++ vector<bool> packs bits. Both are O(T) logical state storage. A full item/target table would require O(nT), while a separately designed bitset implementation could batch word operations.
sections.16: Empty input succeeds only for target zero. Zeros do not create additional reachable totals. Duplicates can be used once per position. A negative number is rejected even when target is zero, because validation precedes the base result. Exhaustive binary selection vectors independently verify small arrays and targets.
sections.18: Only nonnegative values are supported. Resource caps are enforced before allocation. Values are compared against the target, not summed into potentially overflowing totals, so values up to 10^9 remain safe; table indices are at most 10000. The API cannot supply a subset witness or count solutions.

sections.3: Return (sum,start,end-exclusive), or None/null for empty input. Maximize sum, then minimize start, then end. Select a nonempty interval for every nonempty input, including all-negative arrays. Support at most 10000 native integers in [-10^9,10^9]. C++ returns optional<Subarray>; the CLI returns [decimal-sum-string,start,end] to match the existing Divide & Conquer output convention.
sections.8:
Initialize the best result as absent. For each index, start a new ending interval if this is the first element or the previous ending sum is negative; otherwise extend the previous interval. Record a better global candidate by lexicographic preference (-sum,start,end). The endpoint recurrence considers both exhaustive possibilities for an ending interval; induction proves the best sum, and keeping a zero-sum prefix proves the earliest-start tie. Comparing every endpoint with the global result proves the requested final interval and earliest-end tie.

Memoization of E(i) would use a cache and O(n) stack. Full tabulation stores every endpoint sum. Rolling tabulation retains current sum/start and one global interval, yielding constant auxiliary space.
sections.9:
```text
best ← absent; current_sum ← 0; current_start ← 0
for i ← 0..n-1:
    if i=0 OR current_sum<0:
        current_sum ← a[i]; current_start ← i
    else: current_sum ← current_sum+a[i]
    candidate ← (current_sum,current_start,i+1)
    if candidate has better (-sum,start,end) than best: best ← candidate
return best
```
sections.11: Validation and the DP each scan n values once, giving Θ(n+1) time including empty input. Every value order has the same asymptotic work. Each update uses constant fixed-width arithmetic under the shared finite numeric contract.
sections.12: O(1) auxiliary words and O(1) result, with no recursion stack. Input storage is O(n); standalone CLI token/vector allocation is separate from algorithm workspace. Full endpoint tabulation would use O(n), while the existing Divide & Conquer API uses O(log n) recursive frames.
sections.16: Empty input has no interval and returns None/null. [-3,-1,-2] selects (-1,1,2), rather than an empty zero sum. [0,0,0] selects (0,0,1). [0,1] keeps the zero prefix for earlier start. [1,-1,1] retains (1,0,1), the earliest end among equal-sum/equal-start intervals. Exhaustive small ternary arrays and seeded large-magnitude arrays are checked by independent interval enumeration.
sections.18: The shared input cap limits sums to magnitude 10000·10^9=10^13, proving signed-64 additions safe. Python deliberately shares the same finite input domain, whereas the prior Divide & Conquer Python API supports arbitrary integers and its C++ API has wider exact totals. Agreement is asserted on their shared domain. This API does not support circular arrays, all optima, length constraints or streaming mutation.

The recurrences and contracts here are explained independently; no lecture code is copied. The project-specific resource and output contracts are specified in this lesson and its source.

sections.3: prices[i] prices a piece of length i+1; None/null marks an unavailable length. Entries beyond the table are unavailable too. A cut length may be used repeatedly. Return maximum total revenue for pieces exactly summing to length L, or None/null if impossible. L is in 0..10000, k≤1000, k(L+1)≤2000000; available prices are integers in [-10^9,10^9].
sections.8:
R(0)=0; positive lengths start unreachable. For every t increasing, compute R(t)=max(p_c+R(t-c)) over available c≤t with reachable remainder. A feasible partition has some first piece c, and replacing its remainder by a better feasible remainder cannot hurt revenue. Conversely every transition constructs a valid exact partition. Induction proves optimality and preserves impossibility when no transition exists.

Memoization uses the same remaining-length state and O(L) frames in the worst case. Bottom-up tabulation avoids the stack. A single length array suffices; arbitrary available lengths mean two rolling scalars do not suffice.
sections.10:
For prices [2,5,7,8] and rod length 4:

| t | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R(t) | 0 | 2 | 5 | 7 | 10 |
| one optimal first piece | — | 1 | 2 | 1 | 2 |

At t=4, candidates are 2+7=9, 5+5=10, 7+2=9, and 8+0=8. The optimum cuts 2+2. With prices [1,1,1,10], leaving the length-4 rod whole is optimal instead.
sections.11: Let k be price-table length and L rod length. Validation costs O(k); initialization O(L+1); recurrence worst work O(kL), giving O(kL+k+L+1). The Python loop checks all k prices per t; C++ stops once cut length exceeds t. No data-distribution average is assumed. L is numeric, so the method is pseudo-polynomial.
sections.12: O(L+1) auxiliary optional integer cells, O(1) result and no recursion stack. Input storage is O(k). A full piece-count table is unnecessary; returning actual cuts would need predecessor lengths. With a bounded maximum available cut, a rolling window is possible, but the implemented array is clearer.
sections.16: Length zero returns 0, even for an empty price table. Empty prices cannot fill positive length. [None,5] fills length 4 for 10 but cannot fill length 3. Price [-2] at length 3 returns -6, because exact fill is mandatory. None is distinct from the valid price zero. Independent exhaustive ordered compositions check small random inputs.
sections.18: At most L pieces are used, so revenue magnitude is at most 10000·10^9=10^13; signed-64 arithmetic is safe. Dense table/work caps are enforced. The contract excludes discarded leftovers, cut fees, kerf, fractional lengths, limited stock and reconstruction.

sections.3: For a string of at most 1000 Unicode scalar values, return minimum cuts between adjacent positions so every piece is a nonempty palindrome. Empty text returns 0 cuts by convention. Python rejects surrogate code points; C++ decodes strict UTF-8. Symbol equality uses scalar values without normalization, case folding or grapheme segmentation.
sections.8:
P(l,r) is true exactly when the endpoint symbols agree and either r-l<2 or P(l+1,r-1) is true. Process l decreasing so inner intervals are already known. This criterion is correct by removing matching endpoints.

Set Q(0)=0. For e>0, Q(e)=min(Q(s)+1) over 0≤s<e where P(s,e-1). A final piece has one such start s, and optimal replacement of its prefix proves optimal substructure. Every transition forms a valid partition; induction over e proves the minimum. Return Q(n)-1 for n>0 and zero for n=0. Single symbols ensure reachability. Memoization could cache the same interval/prefix states; bottom-up tables avoid stack depth. A separate center-expansion formulation can reduce storage, but this implementation retains the full palindrome table.
sections.10:
For "aab", the palindrome table and prefix costs are:

| l / r | 0 (a) | 1 (a) | 2 (b) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | true | true | false |
| 1 | — | true | false |
| 2 | — | — | true |

| Prefix length e | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Minimum pieces Q(e) | 0 | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| Minimum cuts | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

For e=3, final piece "b" follows the optimal prefix piece "aa", giving two pieces and one cut: aa|b.
sections.11: With n scalars, both palindrome preprocessing and prefix optimization visit Θ(n²) candidate cells for nonempty n. Total time is Θ(n²+n+1), including validation and base cases. C++ strict UTF-8 decoding adds O(B), with B≤4n. Character arrangement changes which minima update, not the quadratic loop counts.
sections.12: O(n²+n+1) auxiliary storage: palindrome membership plus prefix piece counts. C++ also stores n decoded scalars; Python uses the original string. No recursive stack and only O(1) result. Center expansion with a carefully ordered prefix DP is a different O(n)-space approach; two rolling palindrome rows alone do not supply every later prefix query.
sections.16: Empty text returns 0. Any singleton or whole-string palindrome returns 0. All distinct symbols need n-1 cuts. Repeated symbols, odd/even palindromes and Unicode symbols are supported. "😀ব😀" is one palindrome. Exhaustive cut masks with direct reversal checks provide independent expected values, including all binary words through length 7.
sections.18: The 1000-scalar limit bounds the quadratic table. Result and piece counts are at most 1000, so signed-64 arithmetic is safe. No actual partition, deterministic witness tie policy, all-partition enumeration or grapheme-aware segmentation is provided.
